# Case A1 -- volumetric baseline

**Question.** On data generated by the volumetric gas material balance with no measurement
error, does the p/Z inverse recover the gas in place to the precision the arithmetic
allows, and what does that establish?

**Answer.** Yes, and exactly. With a constant deviation factor the recovered gas in place
is `1.000000000000000e+11` scf against a true `1.0e+11` scf: a relative error of exactly
zero, every bit of the double-precision result identical. With a pressure-dependent
Dranchuk-Abou-Kassem deviation factor the error is `+5.40e-14`, against a predeclared
tolerance of `2.0e-11` derived from the conditioning of the extrapolation before the run.
What that establishes is a property of the code, and a narrower property than the zero
suggests: diagnostic D1 below seeds defects into the same arm and finds that a whole class
of them -- any uniform multiplicative error in the ordinate, a wrong standard-volume basis
included -- leaves the recovered G exactly unchanged, so the exact recovery is evidence
only against the classes D1 shows are visible. It is numerical verification, the first of
the three evidence layers in `PLAN.md` section 1. It says the inverse correctly inverts the
forward map on the defects this design can see. It says nothing about whether any reservoir
behaves like the forward map.

Four statements are kept apart throughout this report, and this case reaches only the first:
**numerical verification** (the estimator inverts the forward map to the precision the
arithmetic allows); **conditional pressure reconstruction** (a held-out or reconstructed
pressure series under stated conditions -- not attempted here); **physical interpretation**
(what a reservoir is actually doing); and **decision adequacy** (whether a number is fit to
carry a depletion or development decision). Clearing a tolerance in this case is evidence
about the first only. Separately, `G` and `G - G_p` here are inventory in place; recoverable
gas is a smaller quantity that depends on the drive mechanism and the abandonment condition,
and reserves are a further commercial and regulatory classification of a recoverable volume.
None of the three is presented as another anywhere in this case.

Returning to the headline: the single most useful number in this case is not
the exact recovery at all -- it is the `-5.74` percent error the same estimator produces,
with an R-squared of `0.9971`, when the analyst reuses the initial deviation factor
instead of the pressure-dependent one.

Protocol: `cases/A1_volumetric_baseline/protocol.md`, with every acceptance threshold fixed
before the first execution. Run quoted throughout: `run-006`, snapshot in `results/`,
metrics hash `c45dbaa6ee614460662b16c8bb418ce7218c1610368d49cfb852d4231965f771`, source
commit `855fe54` (working tree dirty: `cases/`, `CHANGELOG.md` and `.gitignore`). Run-006
adds two post-hoc diagnostics, D1 and D2, which are not pre-registered and not gated; it
changed no threshold and no result. Every experiment payload in its `summary.json` is
bit-identical to run-005's, and only the limitation list, the two diagnostic blocks and
therefore the metrics hash differ.

## The setup in one paragraph

A closed tank of 100 Bscf at 4000 psia and 640 degR, produced at a constant 2.5e7 scf/d
and observed at eleven equally spaced times. The forward generator
`reservoir_lab.depletion.simulate_volumetric_depletion` solves, at each step, the implicit
problem `p/Z(p) = (p_i/Z_i)(1 - G_p/G)` for the pressure, by a bracketed safeguarded
Newton iteration, and reports the pressure and the deviation factor separately. The
inverse `reservoir_lab.material_balance.fit_pz_depletion` never sees `G`: it sees eleven
`(G_p, p/Z)` pairs and reports the x-intercept of the least-squares line through them. The
two modules share no code, so a coding slip in one of them does not cancel against the
other. That is the whole of what the separation buys, and it is less than it sounds:
protocol section 3 shows the standard-condition group and the reservoir temperature cancel
identically out of the balance, so a wrong standard-volume basis cannot show up here at
all, and diagnostic D1 confirms it by corrupting that basis by 50 percent and recovering G
with a relative error of exactly zero. For the noise-free runs the comparison does not even
involve least squares: an exactly collinear series is determined by any two of its points,
and the two-point x-intercept computed from the first and last observation alone is
reported alongside.

## Evidence

### 1. Noise-free recovery with a constant Z

Constant `Z = 0.900`, so `p_i/Z_i = 4444.4444` psia and the p/Z line is exactly straight.
Fifty percent depletion, eleven points.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| True gas in place | 1.000000000000000e+11 scf |
| Recovered, `fit_pz_depletion` | 1.000000000000000e+11 scf |
| Relative error | **0.0, exactly** |
| Two-point oracle, no least squares | 1.000000000000000e+11 scf, difference 0.0 |
| Independently coded closed form | 1.000000000000000e+11 scf, difference 0.0 |
| Generator's worst balance residual | 0.0 psia of p/Z |
| Largest fit residual | 9.09e-13 psia |
| Reported standard error | 2.68e-05 scf, i.e. 2.7e-16 of G |
| R-squared | 1.0 |
| Predeclared tolerance | 5.0e-12 |

The tolerance was set in protocol section 5.2 from two terms. The extrapolation's
conditioning is `sqrt(h) = 1.4616` with `h = 1/n + (G - xbar)^2 / S_xx`, so a worst-case
ordinate perturbation is amplified by `sqrt(h n) = 4.8477` before it reaches the
x-intercept; the generator's root finder guarantees only `|dp| <= 1e-12 p`, giving
`4.85e-12`; least-squares rounding over eleven points adds about `1.1e-14`. Budget
`4.86e-12`, gate `5.0e-12`.

The realised error is not merely inside that budget, it is zero, and the reason is visible
in the run rather than inferred: the generator's worst balance residual is `0.0` psia, not
`1e-12`. `_solve_step` warm-starts each step from `required_p_over_z(p_prev) * Z(p_prev)`,
which for a constant Z is the exact root, and `safeguarded_newton` returns immediately on
a residual that is exactly zero. The bracket-width bound was a guarantee, never an
expectation, and the guarantee is what the gate was set from. The bound evaluated at the
residual actually achieved is `0.0`.

The reported standard error of `2.68e-05` scf is the honest consequence of a residual
vector that is rounding noise: `2.7e-16` of the answer. It is not a claim of certainty
about anything.

### 2. Pressure-dependent Z

Same tank, with `Z(p)` the Dranchuk-Abou-Kassem factor at 640 degR on Sutton
pseudocriticals for a 0.65 specific-gravity gas: `T_pc = 365.11` degR, `p_pc = 670.129`
psia. The deviation factor runs from `0.93219` at 4000 psia through a minimum of `0.87972`
to `0.88443` at the last observation, 1897.5 psia.

**2a. Fitted consistently -- and the case brief's expectation was wrong.**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Recovered gas in place | 1.0000000000000539e+11 scf |
| Relative error | **+5.40e-14** |
| Predeclared tolerance | 2.0e-11 |
| Two-point oracle difference | 3.81e-15 |
| Generator's worst balance residual | 1.80e-09 psia of p/Z |
| Conditioning bound from that residual | 2.03e-12 |
| R-squared | 1.0 |

The case brief anticipated that a pressure-dependent Z would bend the p/Z line and produce
a curvature bias in the recovered gas in place. It does not, and protocol section 4.2
recorded that prediction the other way round before the run, with the reason: the tank
balance is `p/Z = (p_i/Z_i)(1 - G_p/G)`, in which the whole standard-condition group and
the reservoir temperature cancel identically. That relation is linear in cumulative
production for *any* `Z(p)` whatever. Curvature does not disappear -- it moves. It lives
in pressure against cumulative production, which is exactly why the p/Z plot exists as an
engineering device. In this run the pressure series departs from the straight line through
its own endpoints by **101.78 psia, 2.54 percent of the initial pressure**. That is the
curvature, it is a real number, and the p/Z transform removes all of it.

What the variable Z does cost is conditioning, and the run measures that too. With a
constant Z the warm start is exact and the generator's residual is zero; with a
pressure-dependent Z the Newton iteration uses a central-difference derivative and leaves
a residual of `1.80e-09` psia. Propagated through the same `sqrt(h n) = 4.8477`
amplification, that bounds the recovery error at `2.03e-12`. The realised error,
`5.40e-14`, sits a factor of 38 inside it. So the honest statement about curvature is: it
takes the generator's own balance residual from exactly zero to `1.80e-09` psia, and the
estimator still recovers G to fourteen figures. Diagnostic D2 repeats the consistent fit on
seven further depletion windows between 1000 and 4000 psia, and the recovery error stays
below `1.5e-13` relative in every one of them, so this is a property of the transform and
not of the one window.

**2b. The inconsistency that does bias G, as a number.**

The mechanism the brief was reaching for is real, but it is not curvature of the balance:
it is a Z that is inconsistent between the reservoir and the analyst. Refitting the same
generated pressures against an ordinate built with the initial deviation factor frozen at
`Z_i = 0.93219` throughout, which is what an analyst does who reads one Z off a chart and
reuses it:

| Quantity | Consistent `Z(p)` | Frozen `Z_i` |
|---|---|---|
| Recovered gas in place | 1.00000e+11 scf | 9.42612e+10 scf |
| Relative error | +5.40e-14 | **-5.7388 percent** |
| R-squared | 1.0 | **0.99706702** |
| Largest residual | 1.71e-09 psia | 73.94 psia |
| Reported standard error | 0.027 scf | 1.284e+09 scf (1.36 percent of the estimate) |
| Fitted `p_i/Z_i` | 4290.99 psia | 4217.05 psia |

Because `Z(p) < Z_i` everywhere below the initial pressure *on this window*, `p/Z_i`
understates the true ordinate by an amount that grows with depletion -- up to **5.63
percent** at the last observation. That tilts the fitted line steeper and pulls the
x-intercept in. The predeclared sign was an underestimate and the predeclared band was 1
to 10 percent; the realised value is `-5.74` percent. Diagnostic D2 shows that the
qualifier in italics is load-bearing: move the window and the sign changes.

Two details deserve attention more than the headline number does. First, the R-squared is
`0.997`, which on a report page reads as an excellent fit, while the answer is 5.7 percent
wrong and 5.7 Bscf short. The library's own warning travels with every fit and says so:
*linearity is not evidence of volumetric drive*. Second, the reported standard error of
1.36 percent does not contain the error. The estimate is 4.5 standard errors away from the
truth, because the standard error describes scatter and this is bias. No uncertainty
band computed from residuals can see a systematic error in the ordinate, which is the
general lesson and the reason `docs/verification_plan.md` says uncertainty from a
structurally wrong model cannot be repaired by a narrower interval.

### 3. Is the reported standard error meaningful

One thousand realisations, constant `Z = 0.900`, independent Gaussian pressure error of 5
psia per point, fifty percent depletion, seeds 1000 to 1999. All 1000 fitted; no
realisation failed, so no filtering rule was needed and none was applied.

| Quantity | Value | Predeclared |
|---|---|---|
| Monte Carlo spread of `G_hat` | 1.793873e+08 scf | -- |
| Mean reported standard error | 1.769719e+08 scf | -- |
| Analytic standard error | 1.827038e+08 scf | -- |
| Spread / mean reported | **1.0136** | in [0.90, 1.15] |
| Mean reported / analytic | **0.9686** | in [0.95, 1.00] |
| Mean relative bias of `G_hat` | -2.95e-05 | abs(bias) <= 5.0e-4 |
| Coverage of the 95 percent t interval | **0.960** | in [0.92, 0.97] |
| Mean Fieller discriminant `g` | 2.89e-05 | -- |

The reported standard error is meaningful: it is within 1.4 percent of the spread it
claims to describe, and the Monte Carlo standard error of a spread over 1000 draws is
itself 2.2 percent, so the two agree within the resolution of the comparison.

The 3.1 percent gap between the mean reported standard error and the analytic value was
predicted before the run and is not a defect. The estimator uses the sample residual
standard deviation on nine degrees of freedom, whose expectation is `c4(9) = 0.9727` times
the true sigma; the observed ratio is `0.9686`. Protocol section 5.4 set the A5 band
around `1.028` rather than around `1.000` for exactly this reason, which is why a gate
centred on unity would have been the wrong gate.

The Fieller discriminant averages `2.9e-05`, four orders of magnitude below the `0.01`
at which a symmetric interval starts to misrepresent the exact set, so the delta-method
linearisation is nowhere near its failure edge here. That is a statement about this design
at half depletion, not about the delta method in general.

### 4. What the x-intercept extrapolation costs

The same eleven noise draws, applied to a history observed to 50 percent depletion and to
one observed to 10 percent. Identical seed, identical point count, additive error in psia,
constant Z -- so the eleven ordinate perturbations are the same eleven numbers, confirmed
by the residual vectors agreeing to `1.36e-12` psia.

| | 50 percent | 10 percent |
|---|---|---|
| Last cumulative production | 5.0e+10 scf | 1.0e+10 scf |
| Final pressure | 2000.0 psia | 3600.0 psia |
| Recovered gas in place | 9.967154e+10 scf | 9.797738e+10 scf |
| Error against truth | -0.328 percent | **-2.023 percent** |
| Reported standard error | 1.7061e+08 scf | 1.0221e+09 scf |
| Relative standard error | **0.171 percent** | **1.043 percent** |
| R-squared | 0.9999550 | 0.9989149 |
| Residual standard deviation | 5.2323754229942 psia | 5.2323754229944 psia |
| Fieller `g` | 2.56e-05 | 6.18e-04 |
| `weak_extrapolation` warning | absent | **present** |

The estimate costs a factor of six in precision for observing a fifth as much depletion,
and the library says so unprompted: at 10 percent the fit carries
`weak_extrapolation: only 10.2% of the fitted gas in place has been produced, so the
x-intercept sits 8.8 data-spans beyond the last observation`.

**The ratio, analytically.** For an ordinary least-squares line the x-intercept variance
collapses to `Var(x0) = (s^2/b^2)[1/n + (x0 - xbar)^2/S_xx]`, so the standard error is
`(s/abs(b)) sqrt(h)`. Three factors can differ between the two arms, and the run reports
each:

* **the residual standard deviation `s`: it does not differ at all.** The hat matrix of a
  straight-line fit depends on the abscissa only through the column space of `[1, x]`,
  which rescaling does not change, and the deterministic ordinate is exactly linear so it
  is annihilated. The two arms report `s` equal to thirteen significant figures. The run's
  ratio is `1.0000000000000344`.
* **the leverage `sqrt(h)`: a factor 6.094.** Evaluated at the true G it is
  `9.0629 / 1.4616 = 6.2005`, which is what protocol section 5.5 predicted because it is
  all a prediction can use. The estimator must evaluate it at the *fitted* x-intercept,
  which is 0.33 and 2.02 percent low respectively, giving `8.8702 / 1.4555 = 6.0942`.
* **the fitted slope: a factor 0.98300.** `SE(slope)` scales as `1/f`, so the 10 percent
  arm's slope is perturbed five times as far by the same noise.

`6.094234 * 0.983003 * 1.000000 = 5.990648`, against a reported ratio of `5.990648`. The
reconstruction reproduces the estimator's ratio to a relative `-1.1e-16`, one unit in the
last place.

The predeclared number was `6.2005` and the realised ratio departs from it by `-3.38`
percent. That is inside the A9 gate of 5 percent and **outside** the `+-1.5` percent band
protocol section 5.5 actually derives. The protocol gives no derivation for the widening
from 1.5 to 5 percent, so A9 has to be read as a regression pin rather than as a gate the
analysis justified: with a gate matching its own derivation, A9 would have failed. The
account of the departure -- leverage evaluated at the fitted x-intercept rather than at the
true G -- is correct arithmetic, it reconstructs the ratio to one ulp, and it was added as
a run-003 diagnostic *after* runs 001 and 002. It is a post-hoc explanation of a prediction
that missed its derived band, not a prediction that was confirmed.

The ratio of the *point-estimate* errors is `6.158`, which was deliberately not gated:
it is `c . e` for one particular noise vector rather than a ratio of norms, and the `1/n`
term enters the two weight vectors identically instead of proportionally.

### 5. What a defect would have to look like to show up here (diagnostic D1)

Post-hoc, not pre-registered, not gated. Experiments 1 and 2a report a recovery error of
zero, and that is evidence of correctness only for defects this design can detect. Nothing
in the case established which those are, so D1 seeds known defects into the experiment-1
arm -- whose uncorrupted error is exactly `0.0` -- and reports what each one costs. A
defect counts as visible if it moves the recovery error past the A1 gate of `5.0e-12`.

| Seeded defect | Class | Magnitude | Recovery error | Visible |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Standard pressure `p_sc` | standard-volume basis | +50 percent | 0.0 | no |
| Standard temperature `T_sc` | standard-volume basis | +50 percent | 0.0 | no |
| Standard `Z_sc` | standard-volume basis | +50 percent | 0.0 | no |
| Reservoir temperature 640 -> 900 degR | reservoir temperature | +40.6 percent | 0.0 | no |
| Whole p/Z series rescaled | ordinate multiplicative | +1e-10 | 0.0 | no |
| Whole p/Z series rescaled | ordinate multiplicative | +1e-03 | 0.0 | no |
| Whole p/Z series rescaled | ordinate multiplicative | +0.5 | 2.22e-16 | no |
| Analyst divides p by 0.8, not 0.9 | ordinate multiplicative | -11.1 percent | 2.22e-16 | no |
| Cumulative production rescaled | abscissa multiplicative | +1e-03 | **+1.000e-03** | yes |
| Cumulative production rescaled | abscissa multiplicative | +1e-02 | **+1.000e-02** | yes |
| First point's p/Z moved | ordinate point-wise | +0.01 psia | **-1.33e-06** | yes |
| Middle point's p/Z moved | ordinate point-wise | +0.01 psia | **+2.05e-07** | yes |
| Last point's p/Z moved | ordinate point-wise | +0.01 psia | **+1.74e-06** | yes |

Three classes, three different answers.

* **Uniform multiplicative error in the ordinate is invisible at any magnitude probed.**
  The x-intercept of a straight line does not move when the ordinate is rescaled, so the
  recovery error stays at or below one ulp even when the series is rescaled by 50 percent
  or the analyst divides pressure by the wrong constant deviation factor. The
  standard-volume basis and the reservoir temperature belong to this class, because they
  enter `p_i/Z_i` and cancel; this is the same cancellation protocol section 3 derives, and
  D1 is its empirical confirmation. Experiments 1 and 2a cannot be cited as evidence that
  the standard basis or the temperature handling is right. Nothing in this case tests them.
* **Multiplicative error in the abscissa maps one for one into G**, with a measured
  sensitivity of `0.9999999999999` and therefore a smallest visible bias of `5.0e-12`
  relative, the gate itself. A 0.1 percent allocation or metering bias in cumulative
  production is a 0.1 percent error in the recovered gas in place, and no experiment in
  this case switches that noise channel on.
* **Point-wise error in the ordinate is visible at `2.88e-08` psia** on the last point,
  from a measured sensitivity of `1.74e-04` of G per psia. The sensitivity depends on which
  point moves, and it changes sign across the design: the first point pulls the intercept
  one way, the last point the other, and a point near the centroid has little leverage.

Experiment 2b is the one large non-uniform ordinate defect the case contains, and read
this way it is a positive control: a Z error that grows with depletion is not
multiplicative and is exactly the shape this design can see, which is why it produces 5.7
percent rather than zero.

### 6. Does the sign of the frozen-Z_i bias generalise (diagnostic D2)

Also post-hoc, not pre-registered, not gated. Experiment 2b's bias is negative because
`Z(p)` falls below `Z_i` across its window. `Z(p)` for this gas at 640 degR has a minimum,
found on a 1 psia grid over [200, 4000] at **2347 psia, `Z = 0.879557`**, and climbs again
below it. So the sign of the bias is a property of where the depletion window sits relative
to that minimum, not of the mechanism. Rerunning the same machinery with the window moved:

| `p_i` (psia) | depletion | `Z_i` | `Z` at last point | frozen-`Z_i` error | R-squared |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4000 | 0.50 | 0.932185 | 0.884427 | **-5.7388 percent** | 0.9970670 |
| 3000 | 0.50 | 0.888955 | 0.896459 | **+0.6076 percent** | 0.9994896 |
| 2500 | 0.50 | 0.880103 | 0.906711 | **+3.1360 percent** | 0.9999189 |
| 2000 | 0.50 | 0.882446 | 0.920337 | **+4.6884 percent** | 0.9999924 |
| 1500 | 0.50 | 0.896976 | 0.937246 | **+4.9816 percent** | 0.9999416 |
| 1000 | 0.50 | 0.922971 | 0.956798 | **+4.0605 percent** | 0.9999291 |
| 4000 | 0.70 | 0.932185 | 0.912690 | -1.9501 percent | 0.9968897 |
| 4000 | 0.90 | 0.932185 | 0.965009 | -0.3037 percent | 0.9977619 |

Below the Z minimum the sign is positive: freezing `Z_i` then *overstates* the ordinate as
depletion proceeds and pushes the x-intercept out. Even at the case's own 4000 psia,
carrying depletion to 90 percent shrinks the bias to -0.30 percent, because Z climbs back
past `Z_i` late in life and the two errors partly cancel.

Two consequences worth stating plainly. First, criterion A4 -- negative, between 1 and 10
percent -- holds for the pre-registered window and for no other initial pressure in this
table: at `p_i = 3000` psia the same machinery gives `+0.61` percent, which fails A4 on
both the sign and the magnitude. A4 is a correct prediction about one configuration and was
not evidence about the class. Second, the consistent-`Z(p)` fit recovers G to better than
`1.5e-13` relative in all eight windows, so experiment 2a's exactness does generalise
across the window in a way 2b's bias does not.

### 7. Determinism and provenance

`summary.json` is byte-identical across repeated executions **on one machine and one
interpreter build** -- Python 3.13.2, CPython, macOS on arm64, as recorded in the run
record: run-001 against run-002 and run-003 against run-004 on the earlier script, and
run-006 against run-007 on the present one. Run-005's `summary.json` is identical to
run-003's.

**A1's prospective ordering is unverified.** This case's `run.py` declares no inputs in its
run record, so nothing machine-written pins `protocol.md` to the runs, and no commit
timestamp separates the two either. Committing a protocol does not establish that it existed
before the run. Cases A2 and A3 do declare `protocol.md` as an input and pin it by SHA-256
inside a record the run itself wrote; that establishes internal content linkage as recorded,
and it is not an independent trusted timestamp and not proof against retrospective
construction. Declaring the protocol as an input in every future `run.py` is what would make
the next case anchored by construction; nothing is retrofitted here.

Nothing here tests reproducibility across platforms, across interpreter builds,
or across versions of `random.Random`'s Gaussian stream, and no claim is made about it.
Criterion A10 is met, by a manual `cmp` between run directories: unlike A1 to A9 it is not
self-checked by `run.py` and does not appear in `summary.json`'s `criteria` block, because
a single execution cannot verify it. Seven numbered run directories exist and none was deleted; the
protocol change log records what changed between them.

## Every predeclared criterion

| # | Criterion | Threshold | Result | Met |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Constant-Z recovery error | <= 5.0e-12 | 0.0 | yes |
| A2 | Two-point oracle agreement | <= 5.0e-12 | 0.0 | yes |
| A3 | Variable-Z recovery error | <= 2.0e-11 | 5.40e-14 | yes |
| A4 | Frozen-`Z_i` bias, negative, 1 to 10 percent | band | -5.739 percent | yes |
| A5 | Spread / mean reported standard error | [0.90, 1.15] | 1.0136 | yes |
| A6 | Mean relative bias | <= 5.0e-4 | -2.95e-05 | yes |
| A7 | Coverage of the 95 percent interval | [0.92, 0.97] | 0.960 | yes |
| A8 | Mean reported / analytic standard error | [0.95, 1.00] | 0.9686 | yes |
| A9 | Extrapolation standard-error ratio | within 5 percent of 6.2005 | 5.9906 (-3.38 percent) | yes |
| A10 | Determinism of `summary.json` | exact | byte-identical, manual `cmp` | yes |

Four entries in that table need reading with their small print, and it is printed here
rather than left to a reader to notice.

* **A9's threshold is not derived.** Section 5.5 derives `6.2005 * (1 +- 0.015)`; the gate
  was written at `+- 5` percent with no stated reason for the widening, and the realised
  `-3.38` percent falls between the two. Treat A9 as a regression pin on the ratio, not as
  a predeclared gate that the section-5 analysis supports.
* **A6 and A7 have no derivation in section 5 either.** They appear only in the section-6
  table. A6 at `5.0e-4` is seventeen times looser than the realised `2.95e-05`, and A7's
  band is about three binomial standard errors either side of 0.95 --
  `sqrt(0.95 * 0.05 / 1000) = 0.0069` -- but asymmetrically rounded, and that arithmetic is
  written down here for the first time, after the fact. Neither shows any sign of having
  been tuned to the answer; neither was derived in advance.
* **A4 is a prediction about one depletion window**, not about the frozen-`Z_i` mechanism.
  Diagnostic D2 gives windows in which the same mechanism fails A4 on sign and magnitude.
* **A10 is checked by hand**, not by `run.py`, and only on this machine.

None of the inconclusiveness conditions in protocol section 8 was triggered: the
generator's residual was resolvable in both noise-free cases, the Monte Carlo landed well
inside its band rather than near an edge, no realisation raised `NotIdentifiableError`,
and the two-point oracle agreed exactly with the least-squares path.

## Limitations

* **This is numerical verification and nothing more.** The generator and the estimator
  share the volumetric assumption set: one tank, constant hydrocarbon pore volume, dry gas
  of fixed composition, isothermal depletion, no influx, no injection, one declared
  standard basis, a volume-averaged pressure at a fixed datum. Agreement between them
  checks the arithmetic. It cannot validate a single one of those assumptions, because
  both sides assert them.
* **The verification is narrower than "the arithmetic is right".** Diagnostic D1 measures
  it: uniform multiplicative error in the ordinate is invisible at every magnitude probed,
  up to +50 percent, and the standard-volume basis and the reservoir temperature fall in
  that class. Experiments 1 and 2a establish nothing about them.
* **Error in cumulative production is never simulated.** `NoiseModel` has four channels and
  only the pressure channel is used anywhere in this case. D1 shows a relative bias in
  `G_p` maps one for one into `G`, which makes allocation and metering bias the most
  consequential untested input in the study.
* **The fit is ordinary least squares, which assumes an error-free abscissa.** Once `G_p`
  carries error the problem is errors-in-variables and OLS is the wrong estimator. The
  library offers Deming and York fits and neither is exercised here, so nothing in this
  case establishes what the reported standard error means when x carries error.
* **Constant hydrocarbon pore volume is asserted, not tested, and water drive is not the
  only way it fails.** Formation and connate-water compressibility -- the abnormally
  pressured, or geopressured, gas reservoir -- curves the p/Z plot and overestimates G with
  no aquifer anywhere in the problem, and it is not represented in the generator at all.
* **Average reservoir pressure is handed to the estimator exactly.** In the field `p-bar`
  is itself an estimate, from a build-up extrapolation (Horner, MBH or MDH) plus a datum
  correction, with model error that is systematic rather than Gaussian, and from a well
  count that may not sample the drainage volume. Nothing here exercises that step.
* **Exact recovery here is fully compatible with the same estimator being badly wrong on a
  real reservoir.** The library's own docstring records a documented weak-water-drive case
  with R-squared 0.9998 and an 8 percent overestimate. Experiment 2b is a scaled-down
  demonstration of the same shape within this case: 0.997 R-squared, 5.7 percent wrong,
  bias 4.5 reported standard errors wide. Demonstrating the drive-mechanism version is
  another case's job.
* **No field data and no published benchmark.** Nothing here is benchmark reproduction and
  nothing here is physical validation.
* **One gas composition, no inerts.** Dranchuk-Abou-Kassem evaluated inside its published
  window, with Sutton pseudocriticals from a 0.65 specific gravity, and no H2S, CO2 or N2,
  so no Wichert-Aziz correction is exercised. [SUPERSEDED] An earlier version of this bullet
  attributed a DAK-against-NIST error of up to 39.7 percent for pure carbon dioxide to
  `scripts/check.py`. That file is the test runner and reports no such figure. The comparison
  belongs to case A2, which reads a NIST reference extract that this repository does not
  redistribute, so the figure cannot be reproduced from this checkout; it is quoted as
  background and no number in this case depends on it. An inert-rich gas
  moves the `Z(p)` trend materially and with it both the magnitude and, per diagnostic D2,
  the sign of the 2b bias. It is not a measured PVT report either, and nothing here
  validates the correlation against one.
* **Dry gas of fixed composition is asserted.** Retrograde condensate dropout, which
  removes liquid from the reservoir gas and changes its composition as pressure falls, is
  outside the generator's model, so no number here speaks to a wet or condensate system.
* **The noise model is the easy one.** Independent Gaussian error per point. Real shut-in
  pressures carry shared calibration bias and temporally correlated error, neither of
  which an independent per-point model represents and both of which the reported standard
  error would understate. The 0.96 coverage in experiment 3 is coverage under the noise
  model that was simulated, not under field measurement error.
* **One design, and the error budget is exact only for it.** Eleven evenly spaced points,
  one gas gravity, one temperature. The even spacing is what makes `xbar = fG/2` and
  `S_xx = 1.1 f^2 G^2` exact, and every leverage, tolerance and predicted ratio in protocol
  section 5 is built on those two identities. Real survey dates cluster in time, and the
  whole budget changes with the spacing.
* **Experiment 2b's number does not transfer, and neither does its sign.** `-5.74` percent
  is specific to this pressure range, temperature and gas gravity. Diagnostic D2 shows the
  sign flips positive once the depletion window sits below the minimum of `Z(p)` near 2347
  psia. What generalises is the mechanism -- an ordinate error that grows or shrinks
  systematically with depletion tilts the fitted line and moves the x-intercept -- not its
  direction.
* **No reserves terminology, development decision or operational limit** follows from any
  number in this case. `G` is an inventory in place. It is not a recoverable volume, which
  would be smaller by whatever the drive mechanism and the abandonment condition leave
  behind, and it is not a reserve, which is a commercial and regulatory classification of a
  recoverable volume. This case establishes numerical verification only; it does not reach
  physical interpretation and it does not reach decision adequacy.

## What would change the conclusion

* A recovery error above the floating-point budget on experiment 1 would mean a defect in
  the regression or the balance, and would stop every case built on them. It would not be
  reportable as a successful recovery with a caveat.
* A disagreement between the two-point oracle and the least-squares x-intercept on exactly
  collinear data would localise a defect to `reservoir_lab.regression`, whichever way the
  recovery error came out.
* If experiment 3's spread-to-reported ratio moved outside `[0.90, 1.15]` on a larger
  ensemble, the delta-method standard error would be miscalibrated for this design and the
  covariance term in `regression.x_intercept` would be the first thing to check.
* Correlated or biased pressure error would break experiment 3's calibration without
  touching experiments 1, 2a or 4. That is the most likely way the reported standard error
  stops meaning what it says, and this case does not test it.
* A defect in the standard-volume basis or in the temperature handling would change nothing
  in any experiment here, by diagnostic D1. Catching one needs a case that compares a
  computed standard volume against an independently computed one, which this is not.

## Library defects found

Two, both at the boundary between the library and the repository's own tooling. Neither
affects any number above.

1. **`provenance.source_revision` writes an absolute repository path into every run
   record, which the repository's own hygiene gate would then reject.** The record carries
   `source_revision.repo_root` verbatim from the caller's argument or, by default, from
   `pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2]`. On any developer machine that is an
   absolute home path, and `scripts/check_repository.py` fails a committed file containing
   it as a `local-leak`. Because `.gitignore` explicitly un-ignores `cases/*/results/` so
   that a case can commit its run snapshot, the documented case workflow would produce a
   record that the documented pre-commit gate refuses. It is worked around at this call
   site by passing `repo_root="."`, which the library accepts without resolving, at the
   cost of requiring the run to be launched from the repository root. With that workaround
   in place the gate is clean -- `python3 scripts/check_repository.py` reported 97 files and
   0 errors when this paragraph was written, and the file count has moved since, as any
   growing tree's will; the load-bearing part is the zero -- and the committed run record of
   every case that has one carries
   `"repo_root": "."`. The defect is in the default, not in the present tree. A library-side
   fix would record the root relative to itself, or omit it: the commit hash beside it is
   the actual identity of the source, and the machine path adds nothing a reader can use.
2. **`simulate_volumetric_depletion`'s default pressure floor sits outside the published
   window of every deviation-factor correlation in `gas_properties`.** The default
   `minimum_pressure_psia = 14.696` is the lower end of the interval the generator scans
   for p/Z monotonicity, so the caller's `z_of_pressure` is evaluated there. For
   Dranchuk-Abou-Kassem with these pseudocriticals that is a reduced pressure of `0.0219`
   against a published range starting at `0.2`, and the correlation emits a
   `RangeWarning`. Under this repository's own policy of treating `RangeWarning` as an
   error -- which `pyproject.toml` sets for the test suite -- the generator does not merely
   warn, it raises `InvalidInputError: z_of_pressure(14.696) raised RangeWarning` before
   any physics runs. Verified directly. This case sets the floor to 200 psia, where the
   reduced pressure is 0.298 and every evaluation is inside the published window; the
   choice is documented in `run.py` and in protocol section 4. A library-side fix would
   either scan from a floor derived from the correlation's own validity window or document
   the default as incompatible with the shipped correlations.

## Plus / minus / recommendation

**Plus.** The estimator is exact on the problem it is meant to be exact on, and the run now
says how narrow that problem is: zero error with a constant Z, `5.40e-14` with a
pressure-dependent one, against tolerances derived from the condition number before the
run rather than from the answer, plus a seeded-defect sweep that reports which defect
classes those zeros could have caught and which they could not. The two-point x-intercept
is a genuinely independent oracle for the noise-free arms -- it uses no least squares at
all -- and it agrees exactly; the separately coded closed form is an independent
*implementation* of the same formula, matching the library's standard error to `1.7e-16`,
which catches a coding slip in one of the two paths and cannot catch a wrong formula. The
reported standard error is calibrated: 1.4 percent from a 1000-realisation spread, with
0.960 coverage. And the extrapolation penalty is not just measured but reconstructed from
its three factors to one unit in the last place. Every number here is reproducible, and the
run is deterministic on this machine and interpreter build.

**Minus.** Every one of those statements is about arithmetic, and diagnostic D1 shows the
arithmetic that is checked excludes a whole class: any uniform multiplicative error in the
ordinate, the standard-volume basis included, is invisible here at any magnitude probed.
The generator and the estimator assume the same physics, so this case is structurally
incapable of catching a wrong assumption, and the one number in it that resembles a real
engineering failure -- the `-5.74` percent from a frozen `Z_i`, at R-squared `0.997`, with
the bias 4.5 reported standard errors wide -- is the one worth remembering, with the caveat
that diagnostic D2 flips its sign as soon as the depletion window moves below the minimum
of `Z(p)`. The noise model is independent Gaussian, the kindest error structure a pressure
survey can have, and the one input that maps one for one into the answer, error in
cumulative production, is never switched on at all. A9's gate is wider than its own
derivation without a stated reason, and A6 and A7 have no derivation at all. The case rests
on a single design: eleven evenly spaced points, one gas gravity, one temperature.

**Recommendation.** Do the cheap structural test before the expensive one. Rerun experiment
3 with `cumulative_gas_relative_sigma` non-zero, then refit the same data with the
library's Deming and York estimators, and report how far the OLS standard error is from the
truth once the abscissa carries error. That is a small change to an existing script, it
attacks the assumption D1 identifies as the most consequential untested one, and it is the
limitation this report is least able to defend. Pair it with `pressure_bias_psia` non-zero
and block-correlated pressure error, which breaks the same interval a second way. After
that, the structural case: generate a history from `simulate_water_drive_depletion`, where
the pore volume available to gas is *not* constant, and fit the volumetric estimator to it
deliberately. If a Cole or pot-aquifer diagnostic is added, it should be added with its
status stated: both are re-plots of the same pressure and production history the p/Z fit
already uses, so neither is an additional independent observation, and both become
informative only to the extent that produced water is separately metered -- which means the
case has to carry a produced-water channel to make them mean anything. Cumulative produced
water at standard conditions, its reservoir-volume equivalent and total influx are three
different quantities, and a case that conflates them will report a diagnostic that looks
stronger than it is. An abnormally pressured depletion case deserves the same treatment,
since it violates the constant-pore-volume assumption with no aquifer present.
